source_user: A long-context workload intermittently hits OOM after several concurrent requests. Give a prioritized diagnosis and mitigations. Scenario variant 39: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure per-request KV growth and allocator fragmentation; check max sequence and batch; inspect active sequences; test paged/prefix cache, admission control, quantization, and context limits.
corrected_answer:
Assumptions and safety: treat this as a device-memory OOM until telemetry distinguishes GPU, host, or swap pressure. Record model, precision, parallelism, allocator/runtime, GPU memory capacity, scheduler limits, maximum context, batch policy, and workload distribution; do not invent missing platform facts. Reproduce first in a bounded staging environment and preserve a known-good configuration.

Prioritized diagnosis and falsifiable hypothesis (scenario variant 39): H1 is that concurrent live KV-cache state plus allocator fragmentation exhausts usable device headroom. It is supported if, at matched prompt/output-length strata, OOM probability increases with measured live KV bytes/tokens and active sequences, and failing runs show a smaller free margin or larger reserved-minus-allocated gap than successful runs. Falsify H1 if OOM occurs with stable bounded live KV and low fragmentation while a non-KV allocation (for example prefill workspace, activations, communication buffers, or a leak) spikes instead. Competing explanations include max-sequence or batch overshoot, duplicated prefix-cache entries, retained KV blocks after completion, and an allocator/runtime regression.

Controlled experiment and measurements: replay a fixed, representative request trace with deterministic seeds where feasible, randomized order, warm-up, and at least repeated runs per prompt-length, output-length, and concurrency stratum. Compare the baseline against one change at a time: (1) bounded admission/concurrency and explicit max context, (2) paged KV and then prefix caching with cache hit/duplication telemetry, (3) KV quantization only if supported and validated, and (4) allocator settings/defragmentation. Log request admission, prefill/decode start and end, active sequences, prompt and generated tokens, per-request and aggregate KV allocated/live/reserved bytes, allocation failures, free/usable GPU memory, reserved-minus-allocated fragmentation, peak non-KV allocations, cache occupancy/evictions, batch size, and OOM stage. After draining requests, check whether live KV returns to baseline and whether reserved memory remains elevated. Define OOM rate as OOM requests divided by attempted requests, and report truncation/rejection separately from successful completions.

Mitigations and decision gates: immediately cap concurrency, maximum sequence length, and KV budget with admission control; reject or queue requests rather than risking process-wide failure, and reserve headroom for non-KV work. Use paged/prefix cache only after measuring its memory benefit and correctness; consider quantization only with output-quality, latency, and stability checks. A mitigation is acceptable only if repeated matched replay has zero unhandled OOMs, no correctness regression, and latency/throughput remain within predeclared SLOs; include confidence intervals or run counts rather than a single lucky run. Roll back on any OOM, correctness failure, unexplained memory retention, latency-budget breach, or unsafe queue growth; canary gradually and keep the baseline available.

Evidence required: allocator and KV telemetry correlated to request IDs, exact workload and limits, repeated baseline/treatment results by stratum, post-drain memory accounting, and logs showing the OOM allocation/stage. Until those are collected, label the causal diagnosis uncertain and use conservative limits.
